problem_statement.title: feat: machine-readable output flag for `tesseract list`
problem_statement.body:
### Summary

Add a machine-readable output flag to `tesseract list` (e.g. `--format json`), so the list of built Tesseract images can be parsed programmatically instead of scraped from the human-facing Rich table.

### Why is this needed?

`tesseract list` currently only renders a Rich table to the terminal. When you want to check *from a script* whether a given image is built — for example, in CI or a build automation step that should fail early with a clear message if a component hasn't been built yet — there's no stable interface.

The only options today are both fragile:

- **Grep the table.** The Name/Tags columns wrap and truncate to terminal width, so a naive `tesseract list | grep <name>` misses matches. You have to force `COLUMNS=1000 tesseract list | grep -w <name>`, which relies on Rich honoring `COLUMNS` and on the column layout not changing between versions.
- **Bypass the CLI** and query the container engine directly (`docker image inspect <name>`), which couples the caller to docker/podman and duplicates image-naming logic that belongs in tesseract-core.

A documented machine-readable flag would give scripts a stable contract and decouple them from both the rendered layout and the container backend.

### Usage example

```bash
$ tesseract list --format json
[
  {
    "id": "sha256:67e3978a5507",
    "name": "mytess",
    "tags": ["mytess:0.1.0", "mytess:latest"],
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "description": "..."
  }
]
```

Enables, for example, an early "is this built?" check without scraping the table:

```bash
tesseract list --format json \
  | jq -e --arg n "$IMAGE" 'any(.[]; .name == $n)' >/dev/null \
  || { echo "Error: $IMAGE is not built"; exit 1; }
```

### Notes

- `json` is the obvious first format; a line-oriented `--quiet` / `--format name` that prints just image names would also cover the "does this exist" check without a JSON dependency.
- Whatever the format, stable field names across versions would let callers rely on them.

problem_statement.title: GREATEST/LEAST → SQLite MAX/MIN silently changes NULL semantics
problem_statement.body:
`GREATEST`/`LEAST` ignore NULL arguments in Postgres and DuckDB. SQLite's multi-argument
`max()`/`min()` return NULL if *any* argument is NULL. sqlglot renames one to the other with
no compensation, so the translated query runs successfully and returns different values.

This is the same bug class as #8283 (`CONCAT` → `||`), which was fixed by routing through
`convert_concat_args`. `GREATEST`/`LEAST` have no equivalent path.

**Read dialect:** `postgres` (also reproduces from `duckdb`)
**Write dialect:** `sqlite`
**Still on main:** yes — `sqlglot/generators/sqlite.py` `least_sql`/`greatest_sql` are a bare
`rename_func("MIN")`/`rename_func("MAX")`. Verified on 30.18.0.

### Fully reproducible code snippet

```python
import sqlite3, sqlglot

sql = "SELECT GREATEST(a, b) AS hi, LEAST(a, b) AS lo FROM t"
out = sqlglot.transpile(sql, read="postgres", write="sqlite")[0]
print(out)          # SELECT MAX(a, b) AS hi, MIN(a, b) AS lo FROM t

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL, 1)")
print(con.execute(out).fetchall())   # [(None, None)]
                                     # Postgres/DuckDB give [(1, 1)]
```

| | `GREATEST(a, b)` | `LEAST(a, b)` |
|---|---|---|
| Postgres / DuckDB | `1` | `1` |
| sqlglot's SQLite output | `NULL` | `NULL` |

### Official documentation

- Postgres, [GREATEST and LEAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-conditional.html#FUNCTIONS-GREATEST-LEAST):
  > NULL values in the argument list are ignored. The result will be NULL only if all the
  > expressions evaluate to NULL. (This is a deviation from the SQL standard. According to the
  > standard, the return value is NULL if any argument is NULL. Some other databases behave this way.)
- SQLite, [max()](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_corefunc.html#max_scalar):
  > The multi-argument max() function returns the argument with the maximum value, or return
  > NULL if any argument is NULL.

  `min()` behaves symmetrically.

### Possible emission

`max()`/`min()` in *aggregate* position skip NULLs, but that form can't be used here — a
subquery in `FROM` can't reference the outer row's columns. Replacing each argument with a
rotation of `COALESCE` over the argument list does work, and needs no new SQLite features:

```sql
-- LEAST(a, b)
MIN(COALESCE(a, b), COALESCE(b, a))
-- GREATEST(a, b, c)
MAX(COALESCE(a, b, c), COALESCE(b, c, a), COALESCE(c, a, b))
```

problem_statement.title: set_env as a list of tables drops every file entry but the last, and ignores the order
problem_statement.body:
`docs/reference/config.rst`, in "References within set_env", documents the list-of-tables form as the way to inherit `set_env` from another environment:

> When you want to inherit `set_env` from another environment you can use the feature that if you pass a list of dictionaries to `set_env` they will be merged together. […] Here the `magic` tox environment will have both `A`, `B`, `C` and `D` environments set.

The entries are flattened into a single dict before being parsed (`src/tox/config/set_env.py:49`):

```python
if isinstance(raw, list):
    self._parse_dict({key: value for entry in raw for key, value in entry.items()})
```

A dict cannot hold the same key twice, and `file` is exactly the key that legitimately repeats, so only the last `file` entry survives. That breaks the documented inheritance pattern itself.

## Reproduction

`base.env` contains `BASE=1`, `extra.env` contains `EXTRA=2`:

```toml
[env_run_base]
package = "skip"
set_env = {file = "base.env", KEEP = "yes"}

[env.magic]
set_env = [
    {replace = "ref", of = ["env_run_base", "set_env"]},
    {file = "extra.env"},
]
```

```
$ tox c -e magic -k set_env
[testenv:magic]
set_env =
  EXTRA=2
  KEEP=yes
  ...
```

`KEEP=yes` is inherited but `BASE=1` is gone, with no warning: the `file = "base.env"` that arrived through `replace = "ref"` was overwritten by the local `file = "extra.env"` during the flattening.

Minimal form, with the INI sibling for comparison:

```
TOML  set_env = [{file = "a.env"}, {file = "b.env"}]   ->  B=2         (A=1 lost)
INI   set_env = \n file|a.env \n file|b.env            ->  A=1  B=2    (correct)
```

## Second symptom, same cause: the order of the entries is ignored

`f.env` contains `FOO=fromfile`:

```
INI    FOO=1 / file|f.env / FOO=2              ->  FOO=2          (the later explicit value wins)
TOML   [{FOO="1"}, {file="f.env"}, {FOO="2"}]  ->  FOO=fromfile   (wrong)
```

A dict keeps a repeated key at the position of its *first* occurrence with the value of the *last*, so `FOO` is pulled back to before the `file` entry and becomes overridable by the file. That contradicts the rule this project already fixed and pinned for INI in `tests/config/test_set_env.py::test_set_env_file_does_not_override_later_values` (#3740).

Both symptoms happen in `tox.toml` and in `pyproject.toml` under `[tool.tox]`.

Notably, the list form exists *because* TOML cannot hold a duplicate key inside one table, so flattening it back into a table undoes the only reason for the form to exist. The existing tests for the list form use distinct keys, so neither symptom was covered.

I have a fix ready (stream the entries in order instead of merging them into a dict first; `_parse_dict` already processes pairs in order and already resets `keys_after_file` at each `file` entry) plus two tests, and will open a PR against this issue.

problem_statement.title: [bug] CMakeConfigDeps silently drops cpp_info.components[...].objects
problem_statement.body:
### Describe the bug

We currently use CMakeDeps and I was trying out CMakeConfigDeps with conan 2.32.0.

We have an internal recipe that exposes a precompiled object file via self.cpp_info.components["objects"].objects = ["/path/to/lib/foo.o"]. It works correctly with CMakeDeps (produces an IMPORTED_OBJECTS  property on the imported target, and the .o ends up in the final link command of any consumer).

With CMakeConfigDeps, the same recipe produces a CMake target for the objects component, but it is an empty INTERFACE IMPORTED library and IMPORTED_OBJECTS  is never set. This is the relevant part in the foo-Targets-debug.cmake file generated.

```
#################### foo::objects ####################
if(NOT TARGET foo::objects)
    message(STATUS "Conan: Target declared imported INTERFACE library 'foo::objects'")
    add_library(foo::objects INTERFACE IMPORTED)
endif()

set_property(TARGET foo::objects APPEND PROPERTY IMPORTED_CONFIGURATIONS DEBUG)
```

Took me a while to figure out because the .o file is silently dropped from every consumer's link line without an error or warning.

Is this intended to be supported at some point? Thanks!

### How to reproduce it

_No response_

problem_statement.title: [Feat]: PushNotificationConfig.authentication is ignored; no Authorization header is sent in push notifications
problem_statement.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

The A2A protocol spec states that when a client provides a `PushNotificationConfig` with an authentication scheme (e.g. `"schemes": ["Bearer"]`), the A2A server **must authenticate** when sending push notifications to the client’s webhook.
Example config:

```json
"configuration": {
  "pushNotificationConfig": {
    "url": "CALLBACK-URL",
    "token": "secure-client-token-for-task-aaa",
    "authentication": {
      "schemes": ["Bearer"]
    }
  }
}
```

However, the Python implementation (`BasePushNotificationSender`) **completely ignores `authentication`** and sends **no `Authorization` header**.
It only attaches:

```
X-A2A-Notification-Token: <token>
```

This means that webhook endpoints cannot authenticate the caller and cannot follow the security model described in the spec.

This appears to be a **spec compliance gap**: push notification authentication is described by the protocol but not implemented in the Python server.




### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like the Python server to:

* Honor `PushNotificationConfig.authentication`
* Support at least the `"Bearer"` scheme
* Automatically add the appropriate `Authorization` header
* Match the spec examples by sending both:

  * `X-A2A-Notification-Token`
  * `Authorization: Bearer <token_or_jwt>`


### Describe alternatives you've considered

As a workaround, we currently:

* **Subclass `BasePushNotificationSender`**
* Override `_dispatch_notification`
* Inject our own `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` header

This works, but:

* It duplicates logic that should be part of the framework
* It breaks consistency between Python and other A2A implementations
* It makes spec-compliant webhook security non-standard and harder to maintain

A built-in implementation would make push notification authentication reliable, consistent, and aligned with the A2A spec.

problem_statement.title: LLMMetadataExtractor fails documents whose extracted metadata contains an "error" key
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

`LLMMetadataExtractor` treats any parsed metadata dict containing an `"error"` key as a failed extraction, even when `"error"` is a legitimate extracted field - including when the user declared it in `expected_keys`.

**To Reproduce**

```python
from haystack.components.extractors.llm_metadata_extractor import LLMMetadataExtractor
from haystack.components.generators.chat.mock import MockChatGenerator
from haystack.dataclasses import Document

extractor = LLMMetadataExtractor(
    prompt="Extract the error type and severity from this log: {{document.content}}",
    expected_keys=["error", "severity"],
    chat_generator=MockChatGenerator(responses=['{"error": "timeout", "severity": "high"}']),
)
result = extractor.run(documents=[Document(content="2026-09-10 ERROR timeout after 30s")])
```

**Actual behavior**

```python
result["documents"] == []
result["failed_documents"][0].meta["metadata_extraction_error"] == "timeout"  # the extracted value!
```

**Expected behavior**

The document lands in `result["documents"]` with `meta == {"error": "timeout", "severity": "high"}`.

**Root cause**

`_extract_metadata` signals parse failure by returning `{"error": <message>}`, and `_process_results` checks `if "error" in parsed_metadata`. A successful extraction whose JSON legitimately contains an `"error"` key is indistinguishable from the failure sentinel. Extracting error/severity fields from logs is a natural use of this component, so the collision is plausible in real pipelines.

**Proposed fix**

Raise an internal exception on parse failure instead of returning a sentinel dict. I have this implemented with regression tests; PR to follow.

**System:** haystack main (post-2.18), Python 3.10

title: fix(repair): refuse a named pipe in the integrity probe (#2498)
issue_title: A named pipe at chroma.sqlite3 stops the MCP server from answering

gold_patch:
diff --git a/CHANGELOG.md b/CHANGELOG.md
index 2638e7fbf7..e667055c8e 100644
--- a/CHANGELOG.md
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
@@ -48,6 +48,7 @@ The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
 
 - **The transcript-path fallback no longer gives every git worktree its own wing.** `_wing_from_transcript_path`'s primary path (reading `cwd` from the JSONL) already collapsed a `<project>/.claude/worktrees/<wt>` segment before deriving the wing; the fallback path, used whenever `cwd` is absent, had no equivalent strip, so the flattened `--claude-worktrees-<wt>` segment survived into the wing name. Applied the same collapse there. (#2388)
 - **`mempalace mine --daemon` no longer mines the daemon's own working directory instead of the caller's.** The daemon is a long-lived background process that keeps whatever cwd it happened to start with, so a relative source (`mempalace mine .`) submitted to it resolved against that stale cwd rather than the directory the CLI call actually ran from, silently mining the wrong project into the wrong wing on every subsequent hook-driven call. `cmd_mine` now resolves the source to an absolute path before it enters the daemon job payload, matching the resolution `_forward_mine_to_hub` already does for the hub-forwarding path. (#2441)
+- **A named pipe at `chroma.sqlite3` no longer stops the MCP server from answering.** The integrity probe opened the pipe for reading, which waits until a writer arrives, and gated tool calls, `mempalace_status`, `mempalace_reconnect` and `/statusz` all run it or wait behind it. Over stdio the first such call left the session answering nothing, `ping` included, until the idle watchdog ended the process; over HTTP those calls hung while `ping` and `/healthz` kept answering. The probe now refuses the pipe by type before any open, as `repair-status` already does, and reports it as an integrity error: gated tool calls get the `-32002` refusal naming it, and `python -m mempalace.repair rebuild` stops at the abort banner instead of hanging. (#2498)
 
 ---

+    A named pipe at ``sqlite_path`` is the one file type answered before any
+    open: opening it for reading parks until a writer arrives, and the probe
+    behind the MCP integrity gate runs under a lock that gated tool calls wait
+    on. It is refused by type, as :func:`sqlite_drawer_count` refuses it, and
+    reported the way an unopenable path is, since the file is not a database.
+    As there, a name swapped for a pipe between the check and the open still
+    parks, since every open after the check goes by name.
     """
+    if _is_a_named_pipe(sqlite_path):

+            f"PRAGMA quick_check failed: {os.path.basename(sqlite_path)} "
+            "resolves to a named pipe, not a database"

     try:

         # sqlite3 module defaults to five seconds, which is shorter than
@@ -902,7 +915,7 @@ def sqlite_integrity_status(palace_path: str) -> SqliteIntegrityStatus:
     # _quick_check_errors, not sqlite_integrity_errors: that one gates on
     # absence again, and a file unlinked between the two gates would come back
     # as an empty list, which is the clean verdict this function exists to
-    # withhold. Past the gate above, only an open attempt may answer.
+    # withhold. Past the gate above, only _quick_check_errors may answer.

problem_statement.title: A named pipe at chroma.sqlite3 stops the MCP server from answering
problem_statement.body:
**What happened?**

If `chroma.sqlite3` in a palace is a named pipe, or a symlink to one, the integrity probe opens it for reading and blocks until a writer shows up, while holding `_sqlite_integrity_refresh_lock`. Gated tool calls, `mempalace_status`, `mempalace_reconnect` and `GET /statusz` all run that probe or wait behind it.

On `develop` @ 38260df5, with a palace whose only entry is that `chroma.sqlite3`:

- stdio: the first `tools/call` for `mempalace_list_wings`, `mempalace_status` or `mempalace_reconnect` gets no answer in 30 s, and a `ping` sent after it gets none in 5 s. The session stays silent until the idle watchdog exits the process, 8 h by default.
- HTTP: the same three tools and `GET /statusz` get no answer in 15 s each, while `ping` and `GET /healthz` still answer.
- `python -m mempalace.repair rebuild` hangs in the same probe.

With an empty regular file in its place, those MCP requests answer within 1 s. `faulthandler` shows the probe blocked in `open(db_path, "rb")` in `config._is_wal_without_sidecars`, reached from `repair._quick_check_errors`. 3.9.0 hangs too, in `sqlite3.connect` in that function.

**What did you expect?**

The probe to refuse the pipe by type before opening it, as `sqlite_drawer_count` does for `repair-status` since #2393, and to report an integrity error. Gated tool calls would then get the `-32002` refusal, `mempalace_status` and `/statusz` would report `ok: false`, and the session would keep answering.

**How to reproduce:**

1. `mkdir /tmp/fifo-palace && mkfifo /tmp/fifo-palace/chroma.sqlite3`
2. Start `python -m mempalace.mcp_server --palace /tmp/fifo-palace` and send `initialize`, then `tools/call` for `mempalace_list_wings`, then `ping`, one JSON-RPC message per line.
3. `initialize` is answered. The tool call and the `ping` are not.

**Environment:**
- OS: Linux (WSL2)
- Python version: 3.12.3 (SQLite 3.45.1)
- MemPal version: `develop` @ 38260df5, and 3.9.0

title: Preserve exact rotations in Clifford+T rebasing
issue_title: [BUG] `rebase(BasisSet.CLIFFORD_T)` silently drops `rx`/`ry`/`rz` gates

 ### Fixed

@@ -69,6 +65,52 @@ def process_gate_statement(cls, gate_name, statement, target_basis_set):
 
         return processed_gates_list
 
+    @classmethod
+    def _get_clifford_t_rotation(cls, statement, gate_name):
+        """Return an exact Clifford+T decomposition for a rotation gate.
+
+        Args:
+            statement: The rotation gate statement to decompose.
+            gate_name: The rotation gate name.
+
+        Returns:
+            list: The exact Clifford+T gate sequence.
+
+        Raises:
+            RebaseError: If the rotation is not an integer multiple of pi/4.
+        """
+        angle = statement.arguments[0].value
+        quarter_turns = angle / (math.pi / 4)
+        rounded_quarter_turns = round(quarter_turns)
+
+        if not math.isclose(quarter_turns, rounded_quarter_turns, rel_tol=0.0, abs_tol=1e-10):
+            raise RebaseError(
+                f"Gate '{gate_name}' with angle {angle} cannot be represented exactly in the "
+                "Clifford+T basis."
+            )
+
+        normalized_turns = rounded_quarter_turns % 8
+        if normalized_turns == 0:
+            return []
+
+        if normalized_turns <= 4:
+            phase_gates = ["s"] * (normalized_turns // 2)
+            phase_gates += ["t"] * (normalized_turns % 2)
+        else:
+            inverse_turns = 8 - normalized_turns
+            phase_gates = ["sdg"] * (inverse_turns // 2)
+            phase_gates += ["tdg"] * (inverse_turns % 2)
+
+        if gate_name == "rx":
+            gate_sequence = ["h", *phase_gates, "h"]
+        elif gate_name == "ry":
+            gate_sequence = ["sdg", "h", *phase_gates, "h", "s"]
+        else:
+            gate_sequence = phase_gates

problem_statement.title: [BUG] `rebase(BasisSet.CLIFFORD_T)` silently drops `rx`/`ry`/`rz` gates
problem_statement.body:
Hi, we're doing some work on testing quantum circuit transformation tools and came across the following issue while evaluating `PyQASM`:

### Environment

- **PyQASM version**: 1.2.0
- **Python version**: 3.10.12
- **Operating system**: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (WSL2)


### What happened?

`QasmModule.rebase(BasisSet.CLIFFORD_T)` silently removes any `rx`, `ry`, or `rz` gate from the circuit. No exception is raised and no warning is printed, the gate is simply gone from the output, and the circuit's measured output distribution changes as a result. This isn't specific to any one angle: for all angles we tested, including `pi/3`, which has no exact Clifford+T representation.

### How can we reproduce the issue?

```python
from pyqasm import dumps, loads
from pyqasm.elements import BasisSet

qasm = """
OPENQASM 2.0;
include "qelib1.inc";
qreg q[1];
creg c[1];
ry(-pi/4) q[0];
measure q[0] -> c[0];
"""

circuit = loads(qasm)
print(dumps(circuit.rebase(BasisSet.CLIFFORD_T, in_place=False)))
```

Output: the `ry(-pi/4) q[0];` line is gone, the `measure` survives untouched. Measuring the input circuit gives `{0: 0.8536, 1: 0.1464}`; measuring this (wrong) output gives `{0: 1.0}` instead.

### What should happen?

The rebase should preserve the circuit semantics, or fail explicitly if the requested operation cannot be represented in the target basis. In this example, `ry(-pi/4)` is exactly representable in Clifford+T; for example, `sdg; h; tdg; h; s` is equivalent up to global phase. The gate should not be silently removed.

### Where does this come from?

In `pyqasm/decomposer.py`, `Decomposer.process_gate_statement` has a branch for `gate_name in {"rx", "ry", "rz"}` whose body is just a comment describing an intended Solovay-Kitaev approximation (`# approx_gates = solovay_kitaev_algo(...)`) followed by `pass`. The function's gate-list accumulator was initialized to `[]` earlier and this branch never populates it, so the gate is dropped. `pyqasm/maps/decomposition_rules.py` has a matching commented-out `solovay_kitaev_algo` stub with a `TODO` above it.

### Suggestions (Optional)

_No response_

problem_statement.title: DeepSeek V4 2-bit DQ fails to load heterogeneous routed projections
problem_statement.body:
## Problem

`deepseek-v4-flash-2bit` fails before inference while loading the catalogued checkpoint. Routed MoE gate and up projections can use different affine quantization group sizes, but the runtime always concatenates their packed tensors into one fused projection. Their packed dimensions differ, so model loading raises a shape mismatch.

A second homogeneous layer exposes an orphaned `up_proj.biases` parameter because the fused path currently combines weight/scales but not quantization biases.

## User impact

The catalog advertises the alias, but Server, CLI benchmark, and downstream GUI launch cannot load it.

## Done when

- heterogeneous gate/up quantization remains as separate projections without changing checkpoint values
- homogeneous layouts retain the fused fast path
- weight, scales, and quantization biases follow the same fusion decision
- focused synthetic tests cover both layouts
- the pinned full checkpoint loads and completes the registered community benchmark protocol

problem_statement.title: ChatPromptBuilder silently drops every content part after the first TextContent
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

`ChatPromptBuilder` accepts a template that is a list of `ChatMessage` objects, and a `ChatMessage` can carry several
content parts (more than one `TextContent`, plus `ImageContent` / `FileContent`). The builder however only ever looks at
`message.text`, which returns the text of the **first** `TextContent` part. Two consequences:

- `run()` rebuilds the rendered message as `replace(message, _content=[TextContent(text=rendered_text)])`, so every
  other content part is silently removed from the rendered prompt;
- `__init__()` infers template variables from `message.text` only, so a variable that lives in one of the dropped parts
  is never reported as a required input.

For a prompt that mixes text and images the generator therefore receives only the first text, and the image just
disappears — with no warning.

**Error message**

None. The failure is silent, which is why it is easy to miss.

**Expected behavior**

Every `TextContent` part of a template message is rendered, non-text content parts are passed through unchanged, and
template variables are inferred from all text parts.

**Additional context**

The same one-part assumption also hides the `templatize_part` filter check for text parts after the first one.

**To Reproduce**

On current `main` (`4354727`):

```python
from haystack.components.builders.chat_prompt_builder import ChatPromptBuilder
from haystack.dataclasses import ChatMessage, ImageContent, TextContent

image = ImageContent(base64_image="cHJldGVuZC1wbmctYnl0ZXM=", mime_type="image/png")
template = [
    ChatMessage.from_user(
        content_parts=[
            TextContent(text="Describe {{ thing }}"),
            image,
            TextContent(text="Also {{ other }}"),
        ]
    )
]

builder = ChatPromptBuilder(template=template)
print(builder.variables)  # actual: ['thing'] -- 'other' is never detected
prompt = builder.run(thing="this", other="x")["prompt"][0]
print(prompt.texts)  # actual: ['Describe this'] -- "Also x" is gone
print([type(p).__name__ for p in prompt._content])  # actual: ['TextContent'] -- the image is gone too
```

**FAQ Check**

- [x] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://docs.haystack.deepset.ai/docs/faq)?

**System:**

- OS: Windows 11
- Haystack version: main @ `4354727`

problem_statement.title: get_default_dataset_io_configurations(backend=None) raises KeyError instead of auto-detecting the backend
problem_statement.body:
`get_default_dataset_io_configurations` documents `backend=None` as "auto-detect from append mode", and its error messages tell the user to "set `backend=None` or remove the keyword argument to allow it to auto-detect". That path cannot be reached: the first line of the function is

```python
DatasetIOConfigurationClass = DATASET_IO_CONFIGURATIONS[backend]
```

so `backend=None` raises `KeyError: None` before any of the detection code runs, whatever the file's state.

```python
from pynwb.testing.mock.file import mock_NWBFile
from neuroconv.tools.nwb_helpers._dataset_configuration import get_default_dataset_io_configurations

list(get_default_dataset_io_configurations(nwbfile=mock_NWBFile(), backend=None))
# KeyError: None   (the intended error is the ValueError asking for a backend)
```

Two smaller things in the same guard block. The check for a file opened read-only uses `nwbfile.read_io.mode`, which `NWBZarrIO` does not expose (the module has `_get_io_mode` for exactly this reason), so a Zarr file read in mode `r` would raise `AttributeError` there. And that check's message says the backend must be specified "if the `nwbfile` is being appended", when it fires precisely because the file is not open for appending.

The lookup should move below the detection block, and the guard should use `_get_io_mode` with a message that describes the case it catches.

problem_statement.title: bug(sdk): get_pipeline_id() does not return pipeline id for private (namespaced) pipelines
problem_statement.body:
### Environment

*  KFP SDK version: 2.17.0

### Steps to reproduce

A pipeline `test-pipeline` was uploaded to namespace `test-ns` as a private pipeline (for the example below, assume its pipeline ID is `a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d`).`get_pipeline_id()` returns `None` for this private pipeline, and it has no `namespace` parameter to search private pipelines. `list_pipelines()` does return the pipeline when `namespace` is specified.

```python
import kfp

client = kfp.Client()

pipeline_id = client.get_pipeline_id(name="test-pipeline")
print(pipeline_id)
# None
# Expected: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
```

```python
shared_pipelines = client.list_pipelines()
print(shared_pipelines)
# Only shared pipelines; test-pipeline is absent (expected)

```

```python
private_pipelines = client.list_pipelines(namespace="test-ns")
print(private_pipelines)
```
Output includes `test-pipeline` (expected):
```
{'next_page_token': None,
 'pipelines': [{'created_at': datetime.datetime(2026, 9, 25, 13, 48, 20, tzinfo=tzutc()),
                'description': None,
                'display_name': 'test-pipeline',
                'error': None,
                'name': 'test-pipeline',
                'namespace': 'test-ns',
                'pipeline_id': 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d',
                'tags': None}],
 'total_size': 1}
```

### Expected result

get_pipeline_id() can return the ID of a private pipeline. Instead it returns None even though the pipeline exists.


### Materials and Reference

`get_pipeline_id()` calls `pipeline_service_list_pipelines` with only a `display_name` filter and no namespace, so it only searches shared pipelines. `list_pipelines()` calls the same API but accepts a `namespace` argument and passes it through, so it can return private pipelines. `get_pipeline_id()` has no way to pass a namespace.

isolated, proxy-configured instance of Chrome or Firefox via

and launch_firefox(), wired into the browser.start dispatcher. I have a
working implementation with tests ready to submit if this is welcome.

problem_statement.title: Chart extraction: `_dataframe_to_tabledata` drops the header row whenever a series label is numeric (years, bins, indices)
problem_statement.body:
**What happens.** The chart2csv output is read with `header=None`
(`granite_vision.py:338`), so the model's header line becomes row 0, and
`_dataframe_to_tabledata` (`:127-190`) decides whether row 0 is a header by

```python
first_row_is_header = all(not self._is_numeric(val) for val in first_row)   # :140
```

Any numeric label in that row — a year, a bin edge, a quarter number, or the `1, 2, 3`
the model emits when it cannot read the legend — makes `first_row_is_header` false. The
header row is then emitted as an ordinary data row with `column_header=False`, and the
grid has no column headers at all.

Concrete case: a bar chart classified at 0.999 came back as

```
Category,1,2,3,4
Institutional,85,15,0,0
Woodlot,10,60,30,0
...
```

Result: 9×5 grid, zero `column_header` cells. For the most common chart x-axis of all —
years — the same thing happens: `Region,2020,2021,2022` is rejected because three of
four labels are numbers.

A second, related issue on the body rows (`:172`):

```python
is_row_header = not self._is_numeric(value)
```

marks *every* non-numeric cell anywhere in the body as `row_header=True`, not only
column 0. A `n/a`, a `—`, or a text category in a middle column becomes a row header.

**Why it matters.** `column_header`/`row_header` are what downstream consumers use to
emit `<th>` / PDF `TH` + `Scope`, i.e. what makes the extracted table accessible. A
chart table with no header row is a grid of bare numbers to a screen-reader user, and
the failure is quietest exactly where charts are most regular.

**Suggested fix.** Two small changes, either sufficient for the common case:

1. Treat row 0 as the header when it is *mixed* (at least one non-numeric cell, e.g.
   `Category`), or when it is numeric but *monotone integer* (years/indices) and the body
   is not. Simpler still: the model is prompted for CSV *with* a header — trust row 0 as
   header unless it is entirely numeric **and** looks like data (same dtype as the rows
   below).
2. Restrict `row_header=True` to column 0 (or to the leading run of non-numeric columns),
   rather than any non-numeric cell.

Happy to open a PR with a unit test over `_dataframe_to_tabledata` covering the four
shapes (all-text header, mixed header, numeric-year header, text cell mid-body) if the
rule above is agreeable.

problem_statement.title: Reduce CPU spent compiling PostgreSQL task-run recorder upserts
problem_statement.body:
### Bug summary

The PostgreSQL task-run recorder embeds every row in its SQLAlchemy upsert with `.values(rows)`. The resulting expression tree grows with the batch, so statement construction and compilation consume substantial recorder CPU before PostgreSQL is called.

In a representative large batch, statement compilation took about 281 ms, and a production CPU profile attributed 60.6% of recorder samples to SQLAlchemy statement construction.

Pass multi-row PostgreSQL segments as execution-time parameters so SQLAlchemy can use its bulk `insertmanyvalues` path. Preserve the existing upsert behavior, and leave SQLite and single-row segments on the existing path.

Prefect defaults to a recorder batch size of 1, so this primarily benefits deployments configured for larger batches.

### Version info

Prefect 3.8.5 and current `main`, PostgreSQL with asyncpg, SQLAlchemy 2.x.

### Additional context

- [PR #22961](https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect/pull/22961) established the same execution-time parameter pattern for the PostgreSQL event persister.
- [SQLAlchemy bulk INSERT](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/queryguide/dml.html#orm-bulk-insert-statements)
- [SQLAlchemy insertmanyvalues](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/connections.html#engine-insertmanyvalues)

problem_statement.title: Bug: `StreamSub` warns that `no_ack` has no effect with a consumer group, but the flag is forwarded to XREADGROUP NOACK
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**

`StreamSub(..., group=..., consumer=..., no_ack=True)` emits

```python
RuntimeWarning: `no_ack` has no effect with consumer group
```

but the flag does have an effect: it reaches Redis as `XREADGROUP ... NOACK`, so entries never enter the PEL. The warning is a leftover from a time when the flag was not forwarded.

**How to reproduce**

```python
from faststream.redis import RedisBroker, StreamSub

broker = RedisBroker()


@broker.subscriber(
    stream=StreamSub("my-stream", group="my-group", consumer="c1", no_ack=True),
)
async def handler(msg: str) -> None:
    ...
```

Constructing the `StreamSub` prints the warning. Running the app shows that the flag is honoured anyway: `XPENDING my-stream my-group` stays empty after messages are consumed.

**Expected behavior**

No warning. `no_ack=True` with a consumer group is a supported, documented mode ("equivalent to acknowledging the message when it is read", see `docs/docs/en/redis/streams/groups.md`).

**Observed behavior**

The warning is emitted in `faststream/redis/schemas/stream_sub.py` (the `elif no_ack:` branch under `if group and consumer:`), while the rest of the code base treats the flag as live:

- `faststream/redis/subscriber/usecases/stream_subscriber.py` passes `noack=stream.no_ack` to `XREADGROUP`;
- `faststream/redis/subscriber/config.py` switches the subscriber to `AckPolicy.MANUAL` when `no_ack` is set;
- `faststream/redis/testing.py` skips the PEL for `no_ack` subscribers;
- #3049 added a `SetupError` for `claim_min_idle_time` + `no_ack`, which only makes sense if `no_ack` works with groups.

**History**

- The warning was introduced in 0.3.5 (#1048), when `no_ack` was indeed not forwarded to `XREADGROUP`.
- #2309 kept the warning and reset `no_ack = False` right after it, so the flag really was ignored for a while.
- 0.6.0 (#1779) dropped that reset, and `noack=stream.no_ack` has been sent to Redis since, but the warning stayed.

The sibling warning, "`no_ack` is not supported by consumer group with last_id other than `>`", is a separate case and should be checked on its own: Redis documents `NOACK` for `XREADGROUP` regardless of the id, so it may be stale too.

**Suggested fix**

Remove the `elif no_ack:` warning branch in `StreamSub.__init__` and add a test asserting that `StreamSub("s", group="g", consumer="c", no_ack=True)` raises no warning and that the subscriber calls `xreadgroup` with `noack=True`. Keep the `claim_min_idle_time` + `no_ack` `SetupError` as is.

**Environment**

Reproduced on `main` (commit 0307f09770).

problem_statement.title: Archive on a cross-profile session fails with misleading "Session not found" (404) instead of 409
problem_statement.body:
## Environment

- hermes-webui browser dashboard served on `http://127.0.0.1:8787`
- Multi-profile setup (at least two profiles), sidebar showing sessions from all profiles
- Local checkout: `adbb3258` (2026-09-17), tag `exp-v0.52.318`, branch master behind origin/master by 101 commits

## Summary

With sessions from other profiles visible in the sidebar, archiving such a session fails with a toast:

> Archive failed: Session not found

The session exists and opens fine (clicking it auto-switches the active profile and loads it). The failure comes from the request-level profile-visibility guard, which reports a profile mismatch as a missing session — the same mismatch that the session detail endpoint reports correctly with HTTP 409.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Have at least two profiles, each with at least one WebUI session.
2. Enable showing sessions from other profiles in the sidebar.
3. Open the context menu of a session that belongs to a non-active profile → **Archive conversation**.

**Actual:** `Archive failed: Session not found`.
**Expected:** the action succeeds (the session is visible and owned by the user), or the server returns a profile-mismatch signal so the client can react meaningfully.

## Wire evidence (captured from the running instance)

```
POST /api/session/archive  {"session_id":"<id>","archived":true}
-> 404 {"error": "Session not found"}

GET /api/session?session_id=<same id>
-> 409 {"error": "Session belongs to a different profile",
        "code": "session_profile_mismatch", "session_id": "<id>", "profile": "def"}
```

Same session id, same moment: the detail endpoint reports a profile mismatch, archive masks it as 404.

## Root cause

`POST /api/session/archive` goes through the generic request guard `_guard_request_session_visibility(...)` (`api/routes.py`, `method="POST"` branch). Inside, `_session_id_visible_to_request_profile()` resolves the session, compares its stored `profile` against the active request profile, and on mismatch calls `bad(handler, "Session not found", 404)` — for a session that was in fact found, just owned by another profile.

Compare with the detail endpoint `GET /api/session`, which handles the identical situation properly (`api/routes.py` ~13028):

```python
if not _session_visible_to_active_profile(_session_profile, handler):
    if _session_profile:
        # Valid session owned by a KNOWN other profile: 409 so the
        # client can offer to switch to it (#5419).
        return j(handler, {
            "error": "Session belongs to a different profile",
            "code": "session_profile_mismatch",
            "session_id": sid,
            "profile": _session_profile,
        }, status=409)
```

Archive has no such branch, so the mismatch is masked as "not found" — which reads like data loss to the user.

## Affected scope

Any mutation that passes `session_id` in a POST/PATCH/DELETE body and is covered by `_guard_request_session_visibility` (e.g. rename, move, pin, delete) presumably behaves the same way. Only archive was verified end-to-end.

## Suggested fix

1. In `_session_id_visible_to_request_profile()` (and/or the guard), distinguish "profile mismatch" from "session missing": return `409` with `code: session_profile_mismatch` and the owning profile for mutations, mirroring the detail-load behavior.
2. Frontend: on `409 session_profile_mismatch` either auto-switch profile before performing the action (consistent with what clicking a cross-profile session in the sidebar already does), or show an actionable error instead of "Session not found".

Auto-switching on click but failing with "not found" on archive is inconsistent UX for the same object in the same list.

---
*Note: this was initially filed against NousResearch/hermes-agent ([#118242](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/118242)) by mistake and closed after the correct repo was identified.*

title: fix(sync): read the directory's identity around a gitignored verdict (#2563)
issue_title: sync --apply removes a drawer when a volume mounted over its directory carries a same-named file and a .gitignore naming it

@@ -58,6 +58,18 @@ The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
 ### Bug Fixes
 
 - **`sync --apply` no longer removes a drawer whose corroborating neighbour is in a different directory than the one its source was mined from.** #2322 made removal ask for a witness in the same directory, which three mount shapes defeat: a mount point whose lower layer holds a mined file of its own, a volume mounted over a directory the palace already knows a file in, and a bind mount of another directory over one it knows, which is what a container does with `-v /host/elsewhere:/project/sub`. Driven through real `mount` and `umount`, all three removed drawers of files that were on disk the whole time. Mining now records which directory each source was read from, as that directory's inode, and `sync` compares it against the inode answering when the verdict is formed. Nothing is written into the source tree for it, so the read-only mounts the README's container recipes use keep working; `st_dev` could not do it, since a bind mount puts both sides on one filesystem where it is the same number. Ten paths record the identity, and `update_drawer` carries it forward when it refiles a drawer as chunks, so every row `sync` can remove holds one. Four bounds: one volume swapped for another at the same path is not separated, a directory deleted and recreated may answer with a different inode and then keeps the drawers of files that really went, a filesystem reporting no inode of its own gains nothing and reproduces the bug in full, and the `gitignored` removal route is unchanged. An existing palace gains the field only as it is re-mined, which `file_already_mined` decides from the stored mtime. Closets are now purged per source a pass emptied rather than per source it removed a drawer from, so a source that kept one keeps the lines that index it. (#2367)
+- **`sync --apply` no longer removes a drawer because a volume mounted over its
+  directory carries a file of the same name and a `.gitignore` that names it.**
+  The `gitignored` verdict was formed from one reading of the path, with nothing
+  to say whose directory answered; #2367 guarded the `missing` verdict beside it
+  with the inode recorded at mine time and listed this route as the bound it

+  identity is removed as gitignored only when the directory answered with that
+  inode before and after the rule was read, and the rules a pass caches are
+  keyed by the identity they were read under, so a rule read from a volume does
+  not decide sources read after the volume left. Anything else is kept and
+  reported as unresolved, as an uncorroborated absence is. A drawer carrying no
+  identity is decided by the rule alone, as before. (#2563)

problem_statement.title: sync --apply removes a drawer when a volume mounted over its directory carries a same-named file and a .gitignore naming it
problem_statement.body:
**What happened?** `sync --apply` removes a drawer whose source file is on disk the whole time, when a volume mounted over the file's directory carries a file of the same name and a `.gitignore` naming it. The `gitignored` verdict comes from one reading of the path, and nothing in it says whose directory answered. The `missing` verdict beside it asks, since #2368, and keeps the neighbour. Measured on `develop` @ e038af97 through the real CLI, with real `mount` and `umount` inside `unshare --mount --map-root-user`, one run each: two files mined from `proj/data`, one drawer each, then a tmpfs over `proj/data`. | what the volume carries | `sync proj --apply` reports | removed | |---|---|---| | a `notes.md` of its own and a `.gitignore` saying `notes.md` | `Gitignored: 1 (removed)`, `Unresolved: 1 (kept)` | `notes.md`'s drawer; `other.md`'s is kept by its recorded identity | | the same `notes.md`, no `.gitignore` | `Unresolved: 1 (kept)` | nothing | | neither file | `Unresolved: 2 (kept)` | nothing | | eight files named like eight mined ones, and a `.gitignore` saying `*` | `Gitignored: 8 (removed)` | every drawer; the palace goes from eight sources to none | After the unmount both files are back on disk, and a search for `notes.md`'s words answers with `other.md`'s paragraph until a re-mine. **What did you expect?** The `gitignored` verdict read like the `missing` one: a drawer carrying the identity `source_identity` records is removed only when the directory answered with that inode before and after the rule was read, and is otherwise kept as unresolved. A drawer carrying no identity is decided by the rule alone, and a rule in the project's own tree keeps removing: with no mount and `proj/data/.gitignore` saying `notes.md`, the run reports `Gitignored: 1 (removed)`, `Kept: 1`. **How to reproduce:** Inside `unshare --mount --map-root-user`, with `

` a scratch palace and `prose` a few lines of text (a one-line file files no drawer). 1. `mkdir -p proj/data && prose > proj/data/notes.md && prose > proj/data/other.md` 2. `mempalace --palace

mine proj` reports `Drawers filed: 2` 3. `mount -t tmpfs tmpfs proj/data && echo generated > proj/data/notes.md && echo notes.md > proj/data/.gitignore` 4. `mempalace --palace

sync proj --apply` reports `Gitignored: 1 (removed)`, `Unresolved: 1 (kept)`, `Removed 1 drawers, 1 closets` 5. `umount proj/data`: both files are back, and `mempalace --palace

mine proj` reports `Drawers filed: 1`. **Environment:** - OS: Linux (WSL2) - Python version: 3.12.3 - MemPal version: `develop` @ e038af97 One of the two reports promised on #2320 once #2367 landed; #2368 names the `gitignored` route as unchanged.

problem_statement.title: Feature: Handover the message for the middleware for the `on_receive` method
problem_statement.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

So implemented a middleware that injects the correlation id  of the message to my loggers via contextvars. Initially I used the `on_consume` and `after_consume` for this. However the issue was that in case an error happend at input validation then my logger wouldn't have the correlation_id since `on_consume` seems to happen after input validation.
So now I'm using `on_receive` and `after_processed`. However for these message I only have access to the middleware via instanceattribute `self.msg`. The issue with this one is the type. In the `BaseMiddleware` we have `self.msg: Optional[Any]`. So since I can't really expect anything from it, I have to do ugly checks for if the msg isn't `None` and of a specific type. 

 
**Describe the solution you'd like**

So it would be more convenient if this function could have a similar interface as `on_consume` or the typing of `self.msg` could be more specific.


**Describe alternatives you've considered**
For now I'm doing the ugly checks :D

```python
async def on_receive(self):
        """Add the correlation id the the context on receive."""
        try:
            if (
                isinstance(self.msg, aio_pika.IncomingMessage)
                and self.msg.correlation_id is not None
            ):
                formated_correlation_id = self.msg.correlation_id.replace("-", "")
                self._token = context.correlation_id.set(formated_correlation_id)
        except Exception as error:
            _LOGGER.error(error)
            # We don't want the middleware to crash the service in case
            # something goes wrong.
            pass
        return await super().on_receive()
```

problem_statement.title: Per-tool timeout_secs is disarmed by an intermediate (is_final=False) result callback — hung async tools are never bounded
problem_statement.body:
## Description

A per-tool `timeout_secs` (and the global `function_call_timeout_secs`) stops protecting a function call the moment the handler reports an intermediate result with `FunctionCallResultProperties(is_final=False)`. In `LLMService._run_function_call`, the shared `function_call_result_callback` cancels `timeout_task` on every delivery — the `is_final` check gates `runner_item.settled`, but the timer cancel below it runs for intermediate updates too:

```python
if is_final:
    runner_item.settled = True

# Cancel timeout task if it exists
if timeout_task and not timeout_task.done():
    await self.cancel_task(timeout_task)
```

An async tool that reports "working on it" a millisecond in — the pattern the docs invite for async function calls — permanently disarms its own deadline. If the handler then hangs, nothing bounds it; a voice caller sits in silence until an idle/silence mechanism ends the call.

The current function-calling docs say a call exceeding `timeout_secs` is cancelled, and that an intermediate result does not close the call — which conflicts with the intermediate result disabling the deadline. No existing issue seems to report this specifically. The closest history: a comment on #4936 ("a valid result callback disables the deadline") and the unmerged PR #5195 built on that rule — but the subsequently merged #5291 semantics and the docs describe the deadline as covering the handler's execution.

Checked on pipecat 1.8.0 and on current `main` (the callback region is identical).

## Deterministic repro

Minimal harness driving `_run_function_call` directly — a handler with `timeout_secs=1.0`, `cancel_on_interruption=False`, that pushes one intermediate update then sleeps 4s:

- **With the intermediate update**: the timeout never fires; the call settles only when the handler returns at ~4.0s.
- **Control (no intermediate update)**: `FunctionCallCancelFrame` with `run_llm=True` is broadcast at ~1.0s, as documented.

Repro script: https://gist.github.com/mannyb223/c71701f2541a83567b5ad560d0f35712

Output (with update):
```
+  0.0s call start (timeout_secs=1.0)
+  0.0s handler start
+  0.0s intermediate update pushed
+ 4.01s broadcast FunctionCallResultFrame     <- only the handler's own late return
```

Control:
```
+  0.0s call start (timeout_secs=1.0)
+  0.0s handler start
+  1.0s broadcast FunctionCallCancelFrame run_llm=True
```

## Suggested fix

Gating the cancel on finality restores the documented behaviour; re-running the repro with this one-line change makes the timeout fire at 1.0s with the intermediate update present:

```python
if is_final and timeout_task and not timeout_task.done():
    await self.cancel_task(timeout_task)
```

If the #4936-comment behaviour (any callback disarms) is actually the intended design, a docs note would help — but then there is no way to bound an async tool that reports progress, which is exactly the long-running shape `timeout_secs` seems built for.

problem_statement.title: Functional model with dict inputs uses an unrelated extra key as the declared input
problem_statement.body:
### Description

A Functional model constructed with dictionary inputs handles a runtime dictionary containing the declared input plus an unrelated feature incorrectly.

Keras warns that the runtime structure does not match, but then attempts to use the unrelated `ignore_feature` scalar as the declared `input_feature` input. This produces a misleading shape error. Constructing the otherwise identical model with an ordered list of named inputs succeeds and ignores the extra runtime key.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

input_feature = keras.Input(shape=(168, 3), name="input_feature")
predictions = keras.layers.Dense(1)(input_feature)

model = keras.Model(
    inputs={"input_feature": input_feature},
    outputs=predictions,
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")

features = {
    "ignore_feature": np.float32(0.0),
    "input_feature": np.zeros((168, 3), dtype=np.float32),
}
targets = np.zeros((168, 1), dtype=np.float32)
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensors((features, targets)).batch(1)

model.fit(dataset, epochs=1)
```

### Observed behavior

```text
UserWarning: The structure of `inputs` doesn't match the expected structure.
Expected: {'input_feature': 'input_feature'}
Received: inputs={'ignore_feature': 'Tensor(shape=(None,))',
                  'input_feature': 'Tensor(shape=(None, 168, 3))'}

ValueError: Invalid input shape for input Tensor("data:0", shape=(None,), dtype=float32).
Expected shape (None, 168, 3), but input has incompatible shape (None,)
```

The invalid tensor is the scalar `ignore_feature`, not the declared `input_feature` value.

Changing only the model input structure avoids the failure:

```python
model = keras.Model(inputs=[input_feature], outputs=predictions)
```

With the named list input, the same dataset trains successfully.

### Expected behavior

Keras should do one of the following:

1. Select the declared input keys by name and ignore extra keys, consistent with the named-list input path; or
2. Raise a clear input-structure mismatch before calling the model.

It should not associate an unrelated extra dictionary value with the declared model input.

### Source-level observation

In Keras 3.12, `Functional._standardize_inputs` reconciles a runtime dictionary by input name when the model's stored input structure is a tensor or list, but not when both the stored and runtime structures are dictionaries. The mismatch is only warned about, after which all runtime dictionary values are flattened and converted against the declared model inputs.

Relevant implementation:
- https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/v3.12.0/keras/src/models/functional.py#L289-L323
- https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/v3.12.0/keras/src/models/functional.py#L243-L249

The current `master` implementation appears to retain the same distinction:
https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/master/keras/src/models/functional.py

### Environment

- Python: 3.12.0
- Keras: 3.12.0
- TensorFlow backend: 2.20.0
- Platform: Linux x86_64

diff --git a/docs/engineering/decisions/2026-09-27-agent-session-prefix-cache.md b/docs/engineering/decisions/2026-09-27-agent-session-prefix-cache.md

@@ -173,12 +173,9 @@ Restart persistence now completes for a realistic session. The newest
 boundary entries are written within the SIGTERM budget and reloaded on start,
 so a client that resumes the same conversation extends them.
 
-Replaying a session from turn 1 after a restart resumes from the newest
-persisted checkpoint below the turn-1 prefix. It does not reuse the full
-turn-1 prefix, because checkpoints are recorded at prefill-chunk strides of
-2048 tokens. An exact turn-1 hit, like oMLX's block-level SSD cache, would
-need one of two follow-ups: a boundary snapshot at the end of system + tools,
-or checkpoints recorded at message boundaries.
+Replaying a session from turn 1 after a restart originally resumed from the
+newest persisted 2048-token stride checkpoint below the turn-1 prefix. The
+#3796 follow-up below adds the exact message-boundary anchor.
 
 Known limits:
 
@@ -192,3 +189,31 @@ Known limits:
   `RAPID_MLX_PREFIX_CACHE_MAX_BYTES` are likewise never raised. Other
   front-ends that build `SchedulerConfig` directly must set
   `cache_memory_percent_explicit` to get the same treatment.
+
+## Follow-up: stable boundary checkpoint
+
+Issue #3796 closes the replay gap by recording the recurrent state at every
+real message-boundary snapshot, independent of the 2048-token stride. The
+first boundary reached by a cold session is marked as its anchor. Checkpoint
+thinning keeps that anchor while still enforcing
+`RAPID_MLX_HYBRID_CHECKPOINT_MAX`; newer stride and message-boundary samples
+compete for the remaining slots. The anchor position is stored in the
+checkpoint sidecar metadata, so later turns after a restart cannot thin it
+away. Internal N-1 snapshots are not session anchors.
+
+Measured 2026-09-28 on an M3 Pro 18 GB with
+`mlx-community/Qwen3.5-9B-4bit`, BF16 KV, MTP, PFlash off, 30 synthetic tool
+schemas, and a fresh cache home:
+
+| Phase | Prompt / cache | Engine TTFT |

problem_statement.title: Restart: replaying an agent session from turn 1 should hit a boundary checkpoint (12 s -> sub-second)
problem_statement.body:
Follow-up to #3794.

**Problem.** After a restart, replaying a Claude-Code-like session from turn 1 is still slow on the 2026-09 harness (scenario c, `after_restart` turn 1, Qwen3.5-9B-4bit):

| Machine | Rapid-MLX with #3794 | oMLX |
|---|---|---|
| M3 Pro 18 GB | 13.2 s | — |
| M4 Pro 48 GB | 12.3 s | 0.27 s |

Before #3794 it took 65-69 s. Resuming the same session (full history plus a new message) already hits at 0.4-0.8 s.

**Cause.** #3794 persists hybrid recurrent-state checkpoints, so a restored entry can serve a shorter shared prefix. The catch is where those checkpoints sit:

- They are recorded at a 2048-token prefill stride, with at most 4 kept.
- The newest one below the turn-1 prefix (22,819 tokens) sits at 18,944, so 3,875 tokens are re-prefilled.
- The exact turn-1 boundary entry was LRU-evicted long before the restart.

**Options:**
1. **Anchor checkpoints at message boundaries.** When a message-boundary snapshot is stored, record a checkpoint at that position too. Stride and thinning would have to keep at least the oldest boundary of a session, which is the end of system + tools.
2. **Take a separate snapshot at the end of system + tools.** That is the stable prefix every turn shares; it would need prompt segmentation at that boundary.

**Out of scope for #3794.** Either option changes checkpoint recording and retention policy. See `docs/engineering/decisions/2026-09-27-agent-session-prefix-cache.md` (Consequences).

problem_statement.title: Polars backend: str col defaults are resolved as col references by add_missing_columns
problem_statement.body:
**Describe the bug**
`add_missing_columns` passes defaults into `with_columns(**{name: default})` as raw values. Polars resolves a bare `str` in that position as a column reference, not a literal. A string default therefore raises `ColumnNotFoundError` — or, if the default equals an existing column's name, silently fills the missing column with that column's values (no error, wrong data). All non-string defaults behave as literals, and the pandas backend adds string defaults correctly.

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandera.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandera.

**Code Sample**
```python
import polars as pl
import pandera.polars as pa

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema(
    {"a": pa.Column(pl.Int64), "unit": pa.Column(pl.Utf8, default="units")},
    add_missing_columns=True,
)
schema.validate(pl.DataFrame({"a": [1]}))
# polars.exceptions.ColumnNotFoundError: unable to find column "units"
```

**Expected behavior**
The missing `unit` column is added with the literal value `"units"`.

**Desktop:**
- OS: Linux
- Version: pandera 0.32.1 (also reproduced on main), polars 1.44.1

problem_statement.title: Improving headers values decoding (utf-8 vs latin1)
problem_statement.body:
This raises from https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/issues/2589 where a server returns a non-UTF-8 header value. According to [this RFC](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7230#section-3.2.4):

>    Historically, HTTP has allowed field content with text in the
   ISO-8859-1 charset [ISO-8859-1], supporting other charsets only
   through use of [RFC2047] encoding.  In practice, most HTTP header
   field values use only a subset of the US-ASCII charset [USASCII].
   Newly defined header fields SHOULD limit their field values to
   US-ASCII octets.  A recipient SHOULD treat other octets in field
   content (obs-text) as opaque data.

So the `latin1` encoding may be preferred over `utf-8` which is the Scrapy's default.  At the other hand, `requests` in some places uses `utf-8` with a fallback to `latin1`: https://github.com/kennethreitz/requests/blob/d6f4818c0b40bc6c00433c013b7daaea83b2cd51/requests/models.py#L908

Following @kmike's [suggestion](https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/2588#issuecomment-282112022), it seems that decoding headers with `utf-8` having `iso-8859-1` as fallback is the best option.
